source: វិធានការចម្រុះគ្រប់គ្រងដំណាំ លើដំណាំស្រូវ (Integrated Pest Management on Rice), training slide deck, Department of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries of Battambang province, presented by Ms. Yem Sophy, Oct 20, 2017 (contact: ysophy168@gmail.com, 012 558 312)
text: Brown planthopper (Nilaparvata lugens) has both long-winged and short-winged adult forms; short-winged females lay more eggs and are associated with populations building up inside a paddy rather than dispersing. Eggs are laid in slits cut into the leaf sheath or midrib, hatch in about 3-8 days, and a female can lay roughly 300-350 eggs. Nymphs cluster low on the plant near the waterline where humidity is high; nymph development takes about 10-12 days and adults live roughly 10-12 days. Populations build up especially fast under warm, humid conditions and heavy nitrogen fertilizer, since lush, closed-canopy growth both feeds the pest and shelters it from natural enemies and insecticide contact. Direct feeding causes yellowing then browning and drying of the whole hill from the base up ('hopperburn'), spreading outward in patches. Brown planthopper is also economically important as the vector of rice ragged stunt and grassy stunt viruses. Natural enemies noted include mirid bugs and phytoseiid predatory mites feeding on eggs and nymphs, plus mymarid, trichogrammatid, and eulophid (Tetrastichus) parasitic wasps attacking the egg stage.
